# New ALTERNATOR + BATTERY yet car STILL won't START! :'(

Replacing major components like an alternator and a battery often feels like flipping the main switch in a complex system, but it doesn't guarantee the application will boot up. In your case with the 2001 Mercedes-Benz E320, you've executed the standard "swap" procedure twice: installing a new alternator after a parasitic drain event, and subsequently installing a fresh battery without success. The fact that the car started via a portable generator jump suggests the engine mechanicals are intact, yet it dies immediately upon driving. This specific symptom profile points away from simple power delivery failure and toward a deeper electrical architecture issue or a failed previous diagnosis.

When a vehicle cranks but dies shortly after start-up, or refuses to crank entirely despite new components, you must treat the battery and alternator as sensors rather than just power sources. The "Check Battery/Alternator" warning light on your E320 is tied directly to the SBC (Self-Contained Battery Charging) module or the internal voltage regulator logic within the alternator itself. If that module failed before the alternator died, simply swapping the unit might not restore functionality if the vehicle's computer has entered a "limp mode" or latched a fault code that prevents ignition.

Consider the architecture of the E320's charging system. It relies on a precise handshake between the battery voltage and the engine control unit (ECU). If the alternator was replaced without clearing existing Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs), the ECU may still believe the system is compromised. The portable generator jump started the car because it provided immediate, high-current power that bypassed the faulty charging circuit long enough to spin the engine. However, once the generator disconnected and the car relied on its own batteryâwhich was likely drained deeplyâthe system failed again because the alternator might not be regulating voltage correctly under load, or the wiring harness connecting the alternator to the ECU is damaged.

Before assuming another expensive part failure, verify the ground straps. On a 20-year-old vehicle, corrosion on the main negative battery terminal or the body ground near the engine block can mimic a dead battery. A high-resistance connection in the ground path prevents the ECU from grounding its internal circuits properly, causing immediate shutdowns when the engine load increases. Use a multimeter to measure voltage drop across the ground strap while cranking; a reading exceeding 0.1V indicates a bad connection that no amount of new parts will fix.

Additionally, check the starter solenoid engagement. If the alternator was installed correctly but the battery was deeply discharged before the second replacement, the battery might not have recovered its capacity even after being charged by the generator. A battery that reads 12.6V at rest but drops to 9V under cranking load is effectively dead and requires replacement, not just a new alternator.

If you have access to an OBD-II scanner capable of reading Mercedes-specific codes, pull the codes now. Look for P0562 (System Voltage Low) or P0614 (ECM/PCM Internal Control Module Performance). These codes confirm whether the issue is purely electrical or if the ECU itself needs attention. If the codes point to a charging system fault even with new parts, investigate the wiring harness for chafing near the alternator belt tensioner, a common failure point on W210 chassis that can sever the signal wire leading to the regulator.

Finally, ensure the new alternator is compatible with the original specifications. Some aftermarket units lack the specific pulley ratio or internal resistance required by older ECU versions, causing voltage spikes that trigger immediate shutdowns. If the wiring and codes are clean, and the battery holds a charge under load, the issue likely lies in the vehicle's internal logic rather than the external components you've swapped.

For further resources on legacy electrical diagnostics, see [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com).
